Macroeconomic.title: Iran sought permission for docking of 3 ships in Indian ports; approval granted: EAM Jaishankar
Macroeconomic.content:
Iran sought India’s permission for three of its ships to dock at Indian ports, with approval granted on March 1 after the request was made on February 28. External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said IRIS LAVAN docked in Kochi on March 4 and its crew are staying in Indian naval facilities. This marked the first instance a senior minister disclosed Iran’s request to dock three ships in India.

One of the three vessels, IRIS Dena, was torpedoed and sunk by a US submarine on March 4 while returning from participation in the Milan multilateral naval exercise and India’s International Fleet Review; at least 87 Iranian sailors were killed. Another Iranian warship, IRIS Bushehr, was permitted to dock by Sri Lanka at Trincomalee after it sought entry due to engine failure.

Jaishankar stressed India’s commitment to energy security amid disruptions in global energy supplies tied to the West Asia conflict. He said the government will maintain energy security by considering availability, costs, and risks in energy markets, while Indian diplomacy supports the country’s energy enterprises. He also detailed advisories issued by Indian embassies in Israel, Iran, the UAE, Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia between February 28 and March 8.

The minister noted the conflict’s escalation has affected normal life and economic activity in the region, with the March 3 call for dialogue and diplomacy reflecting India’s stake in West Asia stability. He highlighted India’s large Gulf-based workforce—about 1 crore Indians—and the region’s importance as an oil and gas supplier.

Civil.title: GE Aerospace to Invest Another $1B in U.S. Manufacturing
Civil.content:
GE Aerospace announced a further $1 billion investment in U.S. manufacturing for 2026, its second consecutive $1 billion U.S. investment. The funds will expand capacity at sites across more than 30 communities in 17 states, accelerate engine deliveries, ramp production of parts that extend time between maintenance shop visits, and strengthen defense production to meet military demand. GE Aerospace plans to hire 5,000 U.S. workers in 2026, in addition to the 5,000 hired last year.

Since 2024, GE Aerospace has announced more than $2.5 billion in U.S. manufacturing investments, including approximately $600 million in sites producing defense engines during the last three years, on top of nearly $3 billion in annual R&D.

Accelerating Deliveries and Capacity
- Cincinnati, Ohio: $115 million to modernize infrastructure, increase test cell capacity, and expand advanced 3D metal printing capabilities.
- Defense: more than $275 million of the $1 billion is for upgrading sites producing defense engines and components.
  - Lynn, Massachusetts: $40+ million for machinery refresh, expanded test cell capacity, and building upgrades.
  - Madisonville, Kentucky: $10 million for new machines, production and inspection tooling, and facility upgrades.

Commercial Engine Growth
- LEAP engine production for Boeing 737 MAX and Airbus A320 families. $200 million to expand LEAP high-pressure turbine durability kits and to support production of the reverse bleed system to reduce on-wing maintenance.
- Durham, North Carolina: $20 million for tooling, engine line assembly systems, and building upgrades.
- Lafayette, Indiana: $7 million for new tools, equipment, and facility upgrades to increase narrowbody engine capacity for 2026 deliveries.

Supply Chain and Workforce
- External supplier base: more than $100 million to provide tooling and equipment to stabilize production schedules.
- The FLIGHT DECK lean operating model helped lift material input from priority suppliers by >40% year over year, contributing to a 25% increase in commercial engine deliveries and a 30% increase in defense engine deliveries in 2025 versus 2024.
- Workforce: GE Aerospace Foundation announced in the fall a $30 million program to train 10,000 workers by 2030.

Note: CFM LEAP engines are produced by CFM International, a 50-50 joint venture between GE Aerospace and Safran Aircraft Engines.

Civil.title: Airbus opens 5,000-seater tech centre in Bengaluru
Civil.content:
Airbus opened a 5,000-seater technology centre on the outskirts of Bengaluru on March 6, 2026. The 880,000-square-foot facility will serve as a hub for engineering, digital transformation, customer services, and procurement, reinforcing Airbus’s Make in India push and India’s growing role in its global value chains. Jürgen Westermeier, president and managing director of Airbus in India and South Asia, described it as a strategic acceleration that provides scale and headroom to grow, ensuring Indian expertise is woven into every stage of Airbus’s global value chains.

The Bengaluru centre is Airbus’s largest engineering and digital centre outside Europe and will support the full lifecycle of aircraft, including maintenance and optimisation of Airbus’s commercial aircraft and helicopter programmes. Indian engineers and digital specialists will work on critical technologies such as cybersecurity, robotics, and AI.

Government and regional officials underscored Bengaluru’s aviation prominence. Minister of Civil Aviation Rammohan Naidu Kinjarapu credited domestic and international confidence in India’s capabilities for the centre. Deputy Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar highlighted the need to build a strong manufacturing presence, not just a market.

Economic impact highlights include Airbus’s India sourcing rising from $500 million in 2019 to over $1.5 billion today, with projections to exceed $2 billion. Airbus collaborates with more than 100 Indian companies supplying components for global aircraft programmes and supports final assembly lines for military transport aircraft and helicopters. Kinjarapu also suggested talks on a second Bengaluru airport.

Civil.title: Embraer Proposes Indian Assembly Line for E175 Jets by 2028 Conditional on Securing at Least 200 Orders
Civil.content:
Embraer is proposing an Indian final-assembly line for its E175-E1 regional jet, potentially starting as early as 2028, but only if it secures at least 200 aircraft orders for production in India. The plan, announced after a memorandum of understanding with Adani Group to establish a local assembly line, hinges on the 200-aircraft threshold. If orders are in place by the end of 2026, Embraer says deliveries could begin in 2028, with an estimated 24-month lead time.

The E175-E1, a seat-88 aircraft, would target India's broad network, with Embraer identifying at least 1,800 Indian routes that could be served by E1s, a key strategic pool given recent demand patterns elsewhere. A India-based plant would also help Embraer boost overall production while allowing the Brazil-based hybrid line to focus on the newer E2 family, which has seen strong global demand.

In terms of milestones, Embraer had targeted 100 commercial aircraft deliveries in 2028 but now suggests the possibility of achieving that milestone in 2027. On the defense side, Embraer regards India as a strategic market for its C-390 military cargo jet, with Mahindra collaborating in India. Saudi Arabia, the EU, and the US were labeled strategic in 2024, but prospects for a Saudi order have dimmed; Embraer is refocusing on India and the United States. A 2023 Lula visit led to a SAMI pact—backed by Saudi PIF—to explore a C-390 assembly line in Saudi Arabia, which remains on the radar but is no longer a hotspot.

Defence.title: Union Minister Piyush Goyal highlights the rapid rise of India’s startup ecosystem in defence, space sectors
Defence.content: On March 7, 2026, at 9:27 AM, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal highlighted the rapid rise of India’s startup ecosystem in the defence and space sectors. He attributed this transformation to the country’s MSMEs, which are integrating Indian innovation into global supply chains. Goyal addressed the 66th cohort of the National Defence College in New Delhi, framing his remarks around the theme “Boosting India’s Manufacturing Sector: Role of Government and Policy.” He stressed that Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s mantra of speed, skill, and scale is a key driver of India’s self-reliance in defence. The minister also emphasized focusing on two strategic sectors—semiconductors and clean energy—to further advance the self-reliance journey. Overall, the speech framed a policy and governance approach that leverages startups and MSMEs to strengthen domestic manufacturing and global supply-chain participation in high-technology domains within defence and space.

Defence.title: India 2nd largest importer of arms in 2021–25, accounted for 8.2% of global arms receipts, think tank says
Defence.content:
SIPRI’s 2021–25 assessment places India as the world’s second-largest arms importer, with an 8.2% share of global arms imports. Although India remains Moscow’s top supplier of weapons during the period, Russia’s share declined to 40% (from 70% in 2011–15 and 51% in 2016–20), as New Delhi shifted its arms sourcing toward Western suppliers, notably France, Israel and the USA. Overall arms receipts declined 4% from 2016–20 to 2021–25, attributed in part to India’s growing domestic design and production capabilities. Top five global importers 2021–25 include Ukraine, India, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Pakistan, collectively receiving 35% of global arms imports.

Defence deals and collaborations highlighted include: an April 2025 Inter-Governmental Agreement with France for 26 Rafale aircraft for the Indian Navy (22 single-seaters, 4 twin-seaters), with training, simulators, weapons, performance-based logistics and extra equipment; delivery due by 2030. India also signed a wet-lease agreement with US-based Metrea Management for one KC-135 (FRA KC-135) for air-to-air refuelling training, to be delivered within six months. Recently, India and France contracted for 26 Rafale-Marine jets. Additional collaborations include Safran–HAL IMRH development and MRO for M88 engines on Rafale, the Scorpène (P75 Kalvari) program with 6th submarine delivered 15 Jan 2025, and continued submarine cooperation. Safran’s JV with BEL to produce HAMMER missiles; Airbus has a H125 Final Assembly Line with ATA Advanced Systems. A Rs 2,182 crore contract with Rosoboronexport for Surface-to-Air Vertical Launch Shtil missiles was signed. A 10-year US–India defence partnership framework positions India as a “priority” defence partner (Pete Hegseth).

Defence.title: Amid conflicts, countries will have to build their industrial complex, upgrade tech: Navy chief
Defence.content:
At Raisina Dialogue 2026 in New Delhi, Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Dinesh K. Tripathi warned that in today’s conflicts, nations must build their own industrial complexes, upgrade technology while producing, and be ready for rapid adaptation. Speaking on a panel titled “Forgers of Peace: Ordnance Factories for the Liberal Order,” he noted that the idea of short, decisive wars is increasingly uncertain, and the post-Cold War peace dividend has “certainly ended.” Countries must prepare for national security by developing their own industrial bases, either independently or with partners, as technology evolves at the “speed of thought.” He urged readiness to surge capacity when required and to adapt quickly.

On sourcing platforms from Russia, Tripathi emphasized India’s commitment to self-reliance while engaging with multiple partners for defence tech via co-development and co-production. He asserted that India is fully aware of how to collaborate with partners and that Russia remains one partner among others. Regarding India’s defence industry, the Navy is pursuing indigenous solutions and niche technologies through structured partnerships, combining indigenous production and development with Make in India, along with co-development and co-production. He expressed optimism that, in coming years, the Indian Navy will become self-reliant.

The event is organized by the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) in partnership with the Ministry of External Affairs. The 11th edition of Raisina Dialogue was inaugurated with Prime Minister Narendra Modi in attendance. Other participants included Lt Gen Susan Coyle of Australia, who highlighted global capacity constraints and deterrence by denial, and Benedikta Von Seherr-Thoss of the European External Action Service, who stressed forging partnerships.

Defence.title: Bengaluru AI warfare & defence startup tests India's first autonomous swarm interceptor
Defence.content:
Bengaluru-based Flying Wedge Defence & Aerospace (FWDA) has tested India’s first autonomous swarm interceptor, FWD YAMA, designed for counter-UAS, air defence and SEAD missions. FWDA claims FWD YAMA can enable aerial interception at up to 100 times lower cost than conventional missile-based air-defence, with a projected unit cost of about $10,000 depending on configuration. The company notes that global conflicts have shown low-cost drones (e.g., Iranian drones under $20,000) can strain high-cost missiles (Patriot systems costing over $4 million per launch), underscoring the need for affordable anti-drone solutions.

FWD YAMA is powered by FWDA’s proprietary autonomy stack and can be integrated across multiple aerial defence platforms, including unmanned systems and precision-guided munitions, enabling autonomous navigation, targeting and engagement. Once cued by radar or surveillance, it can independently detect, classify, prioritise, track and engage aerial threats without human intervention. The system uses radar-based cueing, multi-sensor data fusion, electro-optical and vision-based terminal tracking, and autonomous engagement logic to enable precision interception. It supports coordinated swarm deployment and autonomous distribution of targets, functioning in GPS-denied and electronic-warfare/jamming environments, capable of neutralising threats as small as micro-drones (DJI Mini-class) and scalable to larger unmanned systems.

FWDA says FWD YAMA is designed for airborne integration and has compatibility pathways with its Kaalabhairav UAV series, enabling air-to-air defensive operations and extended engagement ranges, and also supports SEAD roles for autonomous detection and precise neutralisation of hostile air-defence nodes. The development aligns with India’s push for indigenous defence innovation and greater sovereign capability.

Defence.title: West Asia conflict: US President Donald Trump asks defence contractors to quadruple production
Defence.content: West Asia conflict: U.S. President Donald Trump has asked defense contractors to quadruple production to support operations in the West Asia theater. The demand was laid out in a meeting attended by major U.S. defense primes, including Lockheed Martin; RTX (the parent company of Raytheon); BAE Systems; Boeing; Honeywell Aerospace; L3Harris; and Northrop Grumman. The report comes from DH Web Desk and was published and last updated on March 7, 2026, at 03:19 IST. The article does not specify any weapon systems, contracts, or dollar figures, but emphasizes increasing output by four times. The attendee lineup—seven leading companies across defense segments—signals a coordinated, cross-prime push across the U.S. defense industrial base to scale up production in response to the West Asia flare-up. This development underscores the strategic importance of ramping capacity among the major primes as the situation evolves. The absence of program names or funding details leaves specifics on timelines, budget, and order allocations undeclared in this excerpt.

Defence.title: ADA Validates Advanced Intake Aerodynamics for AMCA, Research Achieves 98% Pressure Recovery for Stealth Aircraft
Defence.content:
ADA engineers have reported a major breakthrough in stealth intake design for India’s Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA). In the February 2026 issue of the Journal of Aerospace Sciences and Technologies, ADA researchers—including R. Abilashini and Valliammai Somasundaram—describe an S-duct intake geometry that preserves engine performance while maintaining radar-evading profiles. The work addresses the traditional S-duct challenge of turbulent, distorted flow that can reduce thrust, cause compressor stall, or induce mechanical fatigue.

Key findings include:
- 98% pressure recovery at transonic speeds, ensuring the engine receives dense, stable air for maximum combat power.
- Stable intake performance at a 60-degree angle of attack, with the intake lip generating a controlled vortex that guides flow smoothly into the duct during aggressive maneuvers.
- Validation via wind tunnel experiments and Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD).

Innovative testing methods are also reported. Because full-scale aircraft are impractical for wind tunnels, the team validated using truncated (simplified fuselage) models, showing they can produce 100% accurate intake data if mass-flow instrumentation is properly calibrated. They also developed correction factors to eliminate Sting Interference, improving real-world data accuracy.

Strategic implications are significant: the breakthrough provides foundational data for AMCA and supports the pursuit of sixth-generation tailless blended-wing-body concepts, where stability and stealth are more challenging without vertical stabilizers. This advancement directly strengthens India’s competitive position in next-generation fighter technology.

Defence.title: 13-Ton Ghatak UCAV Receives Critical Development Clearance, Poised to Become IAF's Primary Stealth Strike Platform
Defence.content:
India’s Defence Procurement Board has cleared the design and development of the Ghatak Unmanned Combat Aerial Vehicle (UCAV), a 13-ton class, DRDO-led program that will form the Indian Air Force’s (IAF) future deep-strike and electronic-warfare capability. Positioned as a “first wave” stealth asset, Ghatak is intended to penetrate highly contested airspace before manned fighters and execute Suppression and Destruction of Enemy Air Defences (SEAD/DEAD) missions. Its tailless flying-wing configuration, serpentine air intakes and an internal weapons bay are designed to reduce radar signature and drag, enabling a stealth strike platform with a networked sensor-strike role.

Ghatak will employ an Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) radar and sophisticated electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) sensors to autonomously detect and track targets deep inside enemy territory, functioning as a persistent surveillance node and strike asset. The program traces its lineage to the SWIFT (Stealth Wing Flying Testbed) demonstrator, which completed flight trials in 2022; scaling to a 13-ton heavyweight confirms India’s confidence in tailless flight-control laws.

Propulsion relies on a dry, non-afterburning variant of the indigenous Kaveri engine, delivering about 49 kN of thrust, prioritizing fuel efficiency and long endurance over speed. Performance goals include a combat radius of over 1,000 km, loiter time of 5–8 hours, and an internal payload of around 1.5 tons. By contrast, HAL Tejas Mk1A offers a 300–500 km radius with loiter limited by fuel/pilot fatigue and external payloads of 3.5–5 tons.

Strategically, Ghatak aims to fill the Jaguar’s looming capability gap as it retires over the next decade, enabling high-risk missions without an onboard pilot in initial combat hours and potentially placing India among the U.S., Russia and China in indigenous stealth UCAV capability, with substantial implications for defence manufacturing.
